issues.legal_issue: A High Court may not use supervisory jurisdiction to set aside an interlocutory order merely because it disagrees with the subordinate court’s decision.
material_facts: The trial court allowed the applicants to file a witness list but refused permission to name the opposing side’s advocate as a witness.
The High Court set aside that interlocutory order on the ground that reasons for summoning a witness need not be given, without finding a jurisdictional defect or a resulting failure of justice.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in interfering with the trial court’s order; its order was set aside and the trial court’s order restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution, supervisory or certiorari intervention in subordinate-court proceedings is limited to jurisdictional error, including acting without or in excess of jurisdiction or in flagrant disregard of law or procedure, where failure of justice or grave injustice results. Mere errors of fact or law do not suffice unless the error is manifest and apparent and grave injustice has resulted. The Court applied Surya Dev Rai v. Ram Chander Rai (2003) 6 SCC 675 and Shalini Shyam Shetty v. Rajendra Shankar Patil (2010) 8 SCC 329, which require sparing and disciplined use of supervisory power.

predicates.supervisory_review_of_interlocutory_orde: A party challenges an interlocutory order of a subordinate court through supervisory review.
predicates.manifest_jurisdictional_error: The subordinate court’s order contains a manifest error involving lack or excess of jurisdiction, or a comparable disregard of law or procedure.
predicates.grave_failure_of_justice: The subordinate court’s order has caused grave injustice or a gross failure of justice.

issues.definition: When supervisory review concerns an interlocutory order and the order does not both contain a manifest jurisdictional error and cause grave failure of justice, interference by the High Court is improper.

issues.legal_issue: A court may require a party seeking to summon the opposing party’s advocate as a witness to state the purpose and relevance of the proposed testimony, and may refuse permission when none is disclosed.
material_facts: The respondents applied to add witnesses after filing their written and additional written statements, and included the advocate who had represented the opposing parties throughout the suit.
The respondents did not identify any role the advocate had played in the subject matter of the suit or disclose why his testimony was sought.
The advocate had represented the opposing parties for years, and summoning him without explaining the purpose risked depriving them of his services.
The trial court refused permission to name the advocate as a witness, but the High Court reversed that refusal without addressing the absence of any stated purpose or relevance.
issues.conclusion: The trial court was justified in refusing permission to cite the opposing parties’ advocate as a witness, and the High Court’s contrary order was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Order XVI Rules 1(1) and 1(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure require a party seeking the court’s assistance to procure a witness’s attendance to provide the witness list and the gist of the evidence; Mange Ram v. Brij Mohan (1983) 4 SCC 36 explains that requirement. The court considered it a prudent exercise of discretion to require a brief statement of the purpose for summoning a witness. It also relied on the advocate’s fiduciary duty of utmost good faith and loyalty to the client, the advocate’s duties under Rules 12–15 of Section II, Chapter II, Part IV of the Bar Council of India Rules, 1975, and V. C. Rangadurai v. D. Gopalan (1979) 1 SCC 308.

predicates.civil_trial_witness_list: A party in a civil trial submits a list of proposed witnesses.
predicates.opposing_party_advocate_named_as_witness: The party names as a witness an advocate who represents the opposing party in the proceeding.
predicates.no_purpose_or_relevance_disclosed: The party gives no explanation of the proposed testimony’s purpose or relevance to the dispute.

issues.definition: In a civil trial, when a party names the opposing party’s advocate as a witness without disclosing the purpose or relevance of the testimony, the trial court may refuse to allow that advocate to be called.
